decks.title: The Cell — Part 1: Cell theory, boundaries and the nucleus and organelles
goals: State the main points of the cell theory and distinguish protoplasm from cytoplasm
Compare the cell wall and the cell membrane
State the functions of the nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and Golgi bodies

slides.heading: The Cell: A Unit of Life
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what living things are made of, how a cell is wrapped, and what works inside it.

visual.alt: Flow from cell to tissue to organ to organ system to organism

slides.narration: A banyan tree and a bee look nothing alike, yet both are built from the same kind of tiny unit. Cells join to make tissues, tissues make organs, and organs work together as systems. In this part we look inside one cell.

slides.heading: The cell theory

rows: All organisms are made of cells
One cell or many cells; no living thing is without them
The cell is the unit of structure and function
It is the smallest part that carries out the activities of life
New cells come from existing cells
Cells divide; they do not appear from non-living matter

visual.alt: Table of the three main points of the cell theory

slides.narration: The cell theory has three main ideas. Every organism is made of one or more cells. The cell is the basic unit of structure and of function. And every new cell comes from a cell that already exists.

slides.heading: Protoplasm and cytoplasm

rows: All the living matter of a cell: cytoplasm and nucleus together
The jelly-like part between the cell membrane and the nucleus; holds the organelles

visual.alt: Table distinguishing protoplasm, cytoplasm and nucleoplasm

slides.narration: Protoplasm is the whole living content of a cell. Take out the nucleus and what is left between the nucleus and the cell membrane is the cytoplasm. So the cytoplasm is only a part of the protoplasm.

slides.heading: Quick check: the living content
slides.body_md: Which term covers the cytoplasm and the nucleus together?
slides.narration: Think of the larger whole that contains both.

slides.heading: A generalised animal cell
slides.body_md: An animal cell has a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm** with organelles, and a **nucleus**. There is no cell wall.

visual.alt: A generalised animal cell with its parts labelled

slides.narration: Here is a typical animal cell. The membrane forms its outer boundary. Inside, the cytoplasm holds the organelles, and the nucleus sits near the middle. Notice that there is no wall outside the membrane.

slides.heading: Cell wall and cell membrane

visual.alt: Table comparing the cell wall and the cell membrane on where found, composition, living state, permeability and function

slides.narration: The wall lies outside the membrane in plant cells. It is non-living, made of cellulose, and lets almost everything pass. The membrane is living and selective. It decides which substances may enter or leave the cell.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which boundary?
slides.body_md: A strip of tissue is boiled and its cells stop controlling what enters them, yet the cells keep their shape. Which boundary lost its control?
bullets: Step 1: ask which boundary **controls** entry and exit: the **membrane**.
Step 2: boiling kills the **living** membrane, so control is lost.
Step 3: the **wall** is non-living and freely permeable, so the shape stays.

rows: The cellulose wall is rigid and non-living

visual.alt: Worked table linking each question to the cell membrane or the cell wall

slides.narration: Work through it by asking what each boundary does. Control of entry belongs to the living membrane, and heat destroys it. The wall is a non-living cellulose frame, so the cell keeps its shape.

slides.heading: Quick check: the two boundaries
slides.body_md: Which statement about the cell wall is correct?
slides.narration: Think about whether it is living and what it lets through.

slides.heading: Nucleus and nucleolus

rows: Separates the nucleus and lets materials pass
Dense round body inside the nucleus
Controls the cell and passes on heredity

visual.alt: Table of the nuclear membrane, nucleoplasm and chromatin, nucleolus and the nucleus as a whole with descriptions and functions

slides.narration: The nucleus is the control centre. Its chromatin carries the genes that pass from parent to offspring. Inside it, the dense nucleolus makes the ribosomes, which the cell uses to build proteins.

slides.heading: Mitochondria, ER and Golgi bodies
slides.body_md: **Mitochondria** release energy; **rough ER** carries ribosomes and moves proteins; **Golgi bodies** pack and send out materials.

slides.narration: A mitochondrion has a folded inner membrane for respiration. The rough endoplasmic reticulum is a network of flat sacs covered in ribosomes. The Golgi body is a stack of sacs that packs substances into vesicles.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracing a cell product
slides.body_md: A salivary gland cell makes the enzyme amylase and sends it out. Trace the route.
bullets: Step 1: **ribosomes** on the rough ER build the protein.
Step 2: the **rough ER** carries it inside the cell.
Step 3: the **Golgi body** modifies and packs it into vesicles.
Step 4: vesicles fuse with the **cell membrane** and release it.

visual.alt: Flow of a protein from ribosomes to rough ER to Golgi body to the cell membrane

slides.narration: Follow the enzyme step by step. Ribosomes make it, the rough endoplasmic reticulum carries it, the Golgi body packs it into a vesicle, and the vesicle opens at the cell membrane to release it outside.

slides.heading: Quick check: the powerhouse
slides.body_md: Why are mitochondria called the powerhouses of the cell?
slides.narration: Think about what respiration gives the cell.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cell theory: made of cells; unit of structure and function; cells come from cells.
Protoplasm = cytoplasm + nucleus.
Wall: non-living, cellulose, freely permeable. Membrane: living, selectively permeable.
Nucleus controls; nucleolus makes ribosomes; ribosomes make protein.
Mitochondria release energy; ER transports; Golgi packs.

visual.alt: Summary table giving a one-word job for each organelle

slides.narration: To recap. The cell is the unit of life. The wall protects, the membrane controls, the nucleus directs, ribosomes build protein, mitochondria supply energy, and the Golgi body packs and sends out.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write that the cell wall is **living** or **selectively permeable**.
Say **powerhouse** because mitochondria release **energy** in respiration.
Label diagrams with **ruled lines** that touch the part.
A drawing 6 cm wide of a 60 micrometre cell is magnified **1000 times**: divide drawing size by real size.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Do not call the cell wall living. Explain the powerhouse idea through respiration and energy. Draw ruled label lines that touch the part. And for magnification, divide the size of the drawing by the real size.

slides.heading: Plastids and Cell Types
slides.body_md: Part 2 — organelles of plant cells, and how cells are sorted into two great types.

visual.alt: Flow splitting all cells into prokaryotic cells with no true nucleus and eukaryotic cells with a true nucleus

slides.narration: Cells are not all built alike. Some have a true nucleus and many organelles, and some have neither. First we meet the plastids and a few more organelles, then we compare the main kinds of cell.

slides.heading: Plastids

visual.alt: Table of three plastids with colour and function

slides.narration: Plastids are found in plant cells. Chloroplasts are green and make food by photosynthesis. Chromoplasts hold bright pigments. Leucoplasts have no colour and act as the stores of starch, oil or protein.

slides.heading: Three kinds of plastid
slides.body_md: All three are **plastids**; what a plastid does depends on its **pigment** or contents.

notes.title: The Cell: A Unit of Life — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The cell as the unit of life; cell theory; protoplasm and cytoplasm
sections.body_md:
A **cell** is the smallest unit of structure and function of a living organism. Organisms may be **unicellular** (Amoeba, bacteria) or **multicellular** (a banyan tree, a human). In a multicellular body cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems.

**Cell theory** (Schleiden and Schwann, extended by Virchow):
1. All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic **unit of structure and function**.
3. New cells arise only from **pre-existing cells** by division.

**Protoplasm** is the entire living content of a cell: the **cytoplasm** and the **nucleus** (nucleoplasm) together. The **cytoplasm** is the jelly-like part between the cell membrane and the nucleus; it holds the organelles. (Some books use "protoplasm" and "cytoplasm" loosely; here the ICSE distinction is used.)

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest unit of structure and function of a living organism.
All the living matter of a cell: cytoplasm and nucleus.
The protoplasm outside the nucleus, inside the cell membrane.

visual.alt: Table of protoplasm and cytoplasm

sections.heading: 2. Cell boundaries: cell wall and cell membrane
sections.body_md:
| Point | Cell wall | Cell membrane |
|---|---|---|
| Present in | Plant cells (also fungi, bacteria; composition differs) | All cells |
| Composition | **Cellulose** in plants | **Lipids and proteins** |
| Nature | **Non-living**, rigid | **Living**, flexible |
| Permeability | **Freely permeable** | **Selectively (semi-) permeable** |
| Function | Gives shape, support and protection | Controls what enters and leaves the cell; gives shape to animal cells |

The cell wall lies **outside** the cell membrane. Animal cells have only the membrane.

key_terms.definition_md: Non-living, freely permeable outer layer of plant cells, made of cellulose.
Living, selectively permeable boundary of every cell, made of lipids and proteins.

sections.heading: 3. Nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes and Golgi bodies
sections.body_md:
- **Nucleus:** usually one, bounded by a **double nuclear membrane with pores**; contains **nucleoplasm**, **chromatin** (DNA with proteins, which forms chromosomes) and the **nucleolus**. It **controls** all cell activities and carries **heredity**.
- **Nucleolus:** dense, round body in the nucleus; makes **ribosomes** (and stores RNA).
- **Mitochondria:** rod- or oval-shaped, with an **outer membrane** and an **inner membrane folded into cristae**. They carry out **aerobic respiration** and release energy as ATP, so they are called the **powerhouses** of the cell.
- **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER):** a network of membrane-bound channels. **Rough ER** carries ribosomes and helps make and transport **proteins**; **smooth ER** has none and helps make **lipids** and detoxify. It gives mechanical support and joins the nuclear envelope to the cell surface.
- **Ribosomes:** tiny granules without a membrane, free in the cytoplasm or on rough ER; the site of **protein synthesis**.
- **Golgi bodies:** stacks of flat, curved sacs with vesicles; they **modify, pack and secrete** substances and help form lysosomes.

key_terms.definition_md: Dense body in the nucleus that makes ribosomes.
Organelle with folded inner membrane that releases energy in respiration.
Granule that is the site of protein synthesis.
Stack of sacs that packs and secretes substances.

sections.heading: 4. Plastids, lysosomes, centrosome and vacuoles
sections.body_md:
**Plastids** occur in plant cells (and some protists):
- **Chloroplasts:** green, contain **chlorophyll** in stacks called grana; carry out **photosynthesis**.
- **Chromoplasts:** contain **red, orange or yellow pigments**; colour flowers and fruits.
- **Leucoplasts:** **colourless**; **store** starch (amyloplasts), oils or proteins.

**Lysosomes:** small single-membrane bags of **digestive enzymes**; digest worn-out organelles and foreign matter; called **suicide bags**.
**Centrosome:** near the nucleus in **animal cells**, with two **centrioles**; helps form the **spindle** in cell division. Absent in higher plants.
**Vacuoles:** sacs of **cell sap** bounded by a membrane (tonoplast in plants). Plants have one **large central vacuole** that stores water, salts and food and keeps the cell **turgid**; animal cells have **small, temporary** vacuoles.

key_terms.definition_md: Coloured plastid giving colour to flowers and fruits.
Bag of digestive enzymes; suicide bag.

sections.heading: 5. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
sections.body_md:
| Point | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | **No true nucleus**; DNA lies free as a **nucleoid** (no nuclear membrane) | **True nucleus** with nuclear membrane |
| Organelles | **No membrane-bound organelles** | Mitochondria, ER, Golgi, etc. |
| Ribosomes | Present (smaller) | Present (larger) |
| Size | Usually small (about 1 to 10 micrometres) | Usually larger (10 to 100 micrometres) |
| Examples | Bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) | Amoeba, yeast and other fungi, plants, animals |

Sizes are approximate and differ between books.

sections.heading: 6. Plant cell versus animal cell
sections.body_md:
| Point | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Present (cellulose) | Absent |
| Shape | Usually fixed, regular | Usually irregular |
| Plastids | Present | Absent |
| Vacuoles | One large central vacuole | Small and few |
| Centrosome | Absent in higher plants | Present |
| Nucleus | Often at the side | Usually central |

**Drawing:** draw a generalised cell in outline, then label with ruled lines that touch the part: plant cell (cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus with nucleolus, large vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondrion) and animal cell (membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus with nucleolus, centrosome, Golgi body, mitochondrion, lysosome).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the cell wall **living** or **selectively permeable**.
- Saying protoplasm and cytoplasm are the same thing without the nucleus distinction.
- Drawing a nuclear membrane in a bacterium, or a cell wall in an animal cell.
- Giving "makes energy" for mitochondria: they **release** energy from food (respiration).
- Writing only "powerhouse" without the reason.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a function in one line.
- 2 marks: two differences, each matched point for point; two functions.
- 3 marks: a neat, labelled diagram (one mark for the outline, one for key features, one for correct labels).
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 3, 3 and 4 marks; one part is usually a labelled diagram.

1. The cell wall is **non-living** and made of **cellulose**; the cell membrane is **living** and made of lipids and proteins.
2. The cell wall is **freely permeable**; the cell membrane is **selectively permeable**.

questions.solution_md: Living or non-living; composition; permeability.

questions.stem_md: A cell that must build a great deal of protein has a large, dark nucleolus. This is because the nucleolus

options.text_md: makes the ribosomes on which proteins are built

questions.solution_md: The nucleolus makes ribosomes, the sites of protein synthesis — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into cristae. This arrangement helps the organelle by

options.text_md: forming the spindle in cell division
giving a large surface for the reactions of respiration

questions.solution_md: More folds mean a larger surface for respiration — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Small vesicles filled with secretions bud off from a stack of flat, curved sacs near the nucleus. The stack is the
questions.solution_md: Golgi bodies modify, pack and send out materials in vesicles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT surrounded by a membrane?
questions.solution_md: Ribosomes are tiny granules without a membrane — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A chemical damages the ribosomes of a cell and leaves its other organelles unharmed. Which activity will be reduced most?
questions.solution_md: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sperm cell swims for hours. The middle region behind its head is packed with mitochondria because

options.text_md: the head must digest the egg membrane
the cell must make a large amount of protein
its tail needs a continuous supply of energy

questions.solution_md: Mitochondria release the energy for the beating tail — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A cell of actual width 25 micrometres is drawn 5 cm wide. The magnification of the drawing is
questions.solution_md: 5 cm is 50000 micrometres; 50000 ÷ 25 = 2000 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The folds of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion are called ______.
questions.solution_md: Cristae.

**Assertion (A):** The nucleolus is surrounded by its own double membrane.

**Reason (R):** The nucleolus makes ribosomes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: the nucleolus has no membrane of its own. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the cell organelle, made of stacked flat sacs, that modifies, packs and secretes substances.

answer.model_answer_md: **Golgi body.**

questions.solution_md: Golgi body.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum on one point of structure and one of function.

answer.model_answer_md: **Structure:** rough ER has **ribosomes** on its surface; smooth ER has none. **Function:** rough ER helps make and carry **proteins**; smooth ER helps make **lipids** and remove harmful substances.

questions.solution_md: Ribosomes present or absent; protein or lipid work.

questions.stem_md: Explain why mitochondria are called the powerhouses of the cell. Refer to their structure in your answer.

answer.model_answer_md: Mitochondria carry out **respiration**, which **releases energy** from food. The **inner membrane is folded into cristae**, giving a large surface for the reactions. The energy is stored as ATP and used for all the cell's activities, such as movement and making substances.

questions.solution_md: Respiration, energy release, cristae and use of energy.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a generalised animal cell. Label the cell membrane, nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondrion, Golgi body and centrosome.

answer.model_answer_md: A rounded, irregular outline (**cell membrane**) containing **cytoplasm**; a large central **nucleus** with a dark **nucleolus**; a **mitochondrion** with folded inner membrane, a **Golgi body** of stacked sacs and a **centrosome** of two short rods near the nucleus. No cell wall is drawn.

questions.solution_md: Outline with no wall; six labels.

options.text_md: The nucleus changes into a plastid
Chloroplasts change into chromoplasts with red pigment

questions.solution_md: Green chloroplasts turn into red chromoplasts as the fruit ripens — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A drop of iodine turns the cells of a cut potato tuber blue-black. The starch they contain is stored in
questions.solution_md: Underground storage tissue has colourless leucoplasts that store starch — option (a).

options.text_md: fill with water and make the cells firm (turgid)

questions.solution_md: Water filling the large vacuole makes the cell turgid — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lysosomes are called suicide bags.

**Reason (R):** Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that can digest the cell's own parts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the self-digesting ability of the enzymes explains the name — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Leucoplasts are present in the cells of a potato tuber.

**Reason (R):** Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the reason has nothing to do with why leucoplasts occur in the tuber — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Chloroplast, Chromoplast, Leucoplast, Lysosome.

answer.model_answer_md: **Lysosome**; the others are **plastids**.

questions.solution_md: A lysosome is not a plastid.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the green pigment present in a chloroplast.

answer.model_answer_md: **Chlorophyll.**

questions.solution_md: Chlorophyll.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: lysosomes are called suicide bags.

answer.model_answer_md: Lysosomes hold **digestive enzymes**; if the lysosome bursts, the enzymes can **digest the cell's own parts**.

questions.solution_md: Enzymes can digest their own cell.

questions.stem_md: Name the organelle that helps in cell division in animal cells. State where it lies and the structures that make it up.

answer.model_answer_md: The **centrosome**. It lies **near the nucleus** and consists of **two centrioles**, which help to form the **spindle** during cell division.

questions.solution_md: Centrosome; near nucleus; two centrioles.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of the large central vacuole of a plant cell.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **stores** water, mineral salts and food materials dissolved in the **cell sap**.
2. It keeps the cell **turgid** (firm), which helps to support soft parts of the plant.

questions.solution_md: Storage; turgidity.

questions.stem_md: Cells from the white inner scale leaf of an onion bulb show a wall and a nucleus but no chloroplasts. Give two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: The bulb grows **underground** where there is **no light**, so chlorophyll is not made. Its cells have **leucoplasts**, which **store food** such as starch, instead of chloroplasts.

questions.solution_md: No light; leucoplasts store food.

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of plastid and give one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Chloroplast** (green): traps light for **photosynthesis**.
2. **Chromoplast** (red, orange or yellow): gives **colour** to flowers and fruits.
3. **Leucoplast** (colourless): **stores** starch, oil or protein as a reserve.

questions.solution_md: Chloroplast, chromoplast, leucoplast with functions.

Its respiration takes place in mitochondria
Its proteins are packed by a Golgi body

questions.stem_md:
In a practical class a student scrapes the inside of her cheek, stains the cells with methylene blue and views them under a microscope. A cheek cell is 60 micrometres wide and she draws it 6 cm wide.

(a) Calculate the magnification of her drawing. Show your working. [2]

(b) She also views a peel of onion scale leaf. State two features she sees in the onion cells but not in the cheek cells. [2]

(c) Why do cheek cells have no fixed shape, while onion cells are regular? [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the cheek cell, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Drawing width = 6 cm = 60000 micrometres. Magnification = 60000 ÷ 60 = **1000 times**.

**(b)** A **cell wall** and a **large vacuole** (or plastids in some leaf cells).

**(c)** Animal cells have only a flexible **cell membrane** and no wall, so their shape can change; the **rigid cellulose wall** gives onion cells a fixed, regular shape.

**(d)** An irregular, rounded outline (**cell membrane**) enclosing **cytoplasm**, with a central **nucleus** and a **nucleolus**; a small **vacuole** may be drawn. No wall.

questions.solution_md: Magnification is drawing size divided by real size, 1000 times; wall and vacuole are the plant features; the wall fixes the shape.

questions.stem_md:
A student peels the lower surface of a leaf from a garden plant, mounts it in water and studies 48 cells of the green mesophyll layer under a microscope. Of these, 36 cells show green oval bodies and the rest show none.

(a) What percentage of the cells show the green bodies? [2]

(b) Name the green bodies and the pigment in them, and state their function. [3]

(c) Name one plastid of another colour and one place in a plant where it is found. [1]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a plant cell, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 36 ÷ 48 × 100 = **75 percent**.

**(b)** **Chloroplasts**; the pigment is **chlorophyll**; they trap light for **photosynthesis**.

**(c)** **Chromoplast** in a ripe tomato or a petal (or **leucoplast** in a potato tuber).

**(d)** A rectangular outline with **cell wall** and **cell membrane**; **large vacuole**; **nucleus**; **chloroplasts** in the cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: 75 percent; chloroplast, chlorophyll, photosynthesis; chromoplast; labelled plant cell.

marking_scheme.step: Rectangular cell with wall and vacuole

questions.stem_md:
A cell lining the wall of the stomach makes the enzyme pepsin, which is a protein, and releases it into the stomach.

(a) Name, in order, the organelles through which the pepsin passes from its making to its release. [3]

(b) The cell needs a great deal of energy for this work. Name the organelle that supplies it and the process involved. [2]

(c) State what would happen to the cell's ability to make pepsin if its nucleolus failed to work. Give a reason. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a Golgi body. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Ribosomes** (build the protein) → **rough endoplasmic reticulum** (carries it) → **Golgi body** (modifies and packs it into vesicles) → **cell membrane** (releases it).

**(b)** The **mitochondria**, by **respiration**, which releases energy from food.

(c) The cell could not make enough pepsin, because the **nucleolus makes ribosomes**, and without ribosomes proteins cannot be built.

**(d)** A stack of four or five **flat, curved sacs** one above another, with small **vesicles** budding from the edges; labelled **Golgi body**, **sacs** and **vesicles**.

questions.solution_md: Ribosome, rough ER, Golgi body, cell membrane; mitochondria and respiration; nucleolus makes ribosomes; labelled Golgi body.

questions.stem_md:
A student studies two cells under an electron microscope. Cell P has a wall, ribosomes and DNA lying free in the cytoplasm, but no nuclear membrane and no mitochondria. Cell Q has a cellulose wall, a nucleus, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

(a) Name the type of cell each is and give one reason for each. [3]

(b) Name one structure present in both P and Q. [1]

(c) Tabulate two differences between P and Q other than those in the description. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of cell P, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** P is **prokaryotic** (no nuclear membrane; DNA free). Q is **eukaryotic** (has a true nucleus bounded by a membrane); Q is also a **plant cell** (cellulose wall, chloroplasts).

**(b)** **Ribosomes** (or a cell wall, or a cell membrane).

**(c)** | P | Q |
|---|---|
| Usually very small | Larger |
| Has a **nucleoid** and may carry **plasmids** | Has chromosomes inside a nucleus |

**(d)** A rod-shaped outline with **cell wall**, **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm** with **ribosomes**, a **nucleoid** (coiled DNA) and possibly a **flagellum**; no nucleus or organelles drawn.

questions.solution_md: P prokaryotic, Q eukaryotic; ribosomes common; size and DNA arrangement differ; labelled bacterium.

questions.stem_md:
A white blood cell of the human body engulfs a bacterium, enclosing it in a vesicle. Enzymes then break the bacterium down.

(a) Name the organelle that supplies the enzymes and explain why it is called a suicide bag. [2]

(b) The white blood cell must move and engulf the bacterium. Name the organelle that supplies its energy and the process. [2]

(c) State three ways in which the structure of the bacterium differs from that of the white blood cell. [3]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a mitochondrion. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **lysosome**; its **digestive enzymes** can digest the cell's own parts if the bag bursts.

**(b)** The **mitochondria**, by **respiration**.

**(c)** The bacterium has **no true nucleus** (nucleoid only); **no membrane-bound organelles**; it has a **cell wall**, which the white blood cell lacks; it is much **smaller**. (any three)

**(d)** An **oval** body with a smooth **outer membrane** and an **inner membrane folded into cristae**; the space inside is the matrix.

questions.solution_md: Lysosome; mitochondria and respiration; three prokaryote differences; labelled mitochondrion.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of a plant cell. Parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A and E and state one difference between them. [3]

(b) A student says that the cell in the diagram could not belong to an animal. Give three structural reasons that support her. [3]

(c) The part marked C is missing from the cells of a plant grown in the dark. State the effect on the plant and give a reason. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an animal cell, showing two structures that the cell in the diagram does not have. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is the **cell wall**; E is the **cell membrane**. The wall is **non-living and freely permeable**; the membrane is **living and selectively permeable**.

**(b)** It has a **cell wall**, a **large central vacuole** and **plastids (chloroplasts)**; an animal cell has none of these. (any three)

**(c)** C is a **chloroplast**. Without it the plant cannot **photosynthesise**, so it would be pale and could not make its own food.

**(d)** A rounded outline with membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm, and a **centrosome** and **small vacuoles** (or lysosomes), which the plant cell does not show.

questions.solution_md: A cell wall, E cell membrane; wall, vacuole, plastids absent in animals; chloroplast photosynthesis; animal cell with centrosome.
